chapter_theme: Under the heading ஈகை, fifteen verses on giving: giving to get more is angling, the hoard ends with the king while a small gift to the starving is rain in the waste, discerning giving neither drains nor dwindles wealth but renews it like tank and well, the best giver reads the need, the habitual giver gives even in want as Pari's daughter did in drought, a gift measures the patron's worth, giving for fame is wage work, crowds of askers and incapable patrons defeat the asker, and wealth not given in time is lost past remedy.

372.reading: Those who give a small thing and by that act look to gain a large one are, the verse tells the lord of the river town where spread flowers mingle in the water, like anglers who throw away the small ayirai fish to haul in the varal.
372.nuance: The verse does not call such giving wrong in so many words; the angler's image makes it plain that the gift is bait and the giving a kind of trade. Its place under the heading ஈகை implies the censure.

pazhamozhi.literal: they are those who let go the ayirai they wanted and pull in the varal

story.act: no story; the angler who sacrifices a small fish as bait to land a bigger one

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving a little in order to get much back is fishing, not giving

373.reading: What the concealers have laid up helps no one in the end except as a provision for kings who drive them out and seize it, while giving even one thing to help those crushed by want is rain falling in the dry wilderness.
373.nuance: The verse sets two ends of wealth side by side: the hoard feeds the seizing king, the small gift feeds the destitute. துரப்புடைய may mean kings given to driving people out or to pursuing; either way the hoard passes to royal power.

pazhamozhi.literal: rain poured in the middle of the dry wilderness

story.act: no story; rain in the wasteland stands for a gift where need is greatest

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a small gift to those in deep want is worth more than any hoard

374.reading: Wealth that lay gathered over many years and idle, once a capable man gives it out with discernment, does not quickly run dry, any more than the water a tank has long held runs out.
374.nuance: The giver must be வல்லான் and must give தெரிந்து, with discernment: the claim that giving does not exhaust wealth is made for discerning giving, not for any scattering. வல்லே (quickly) qualifies the running out.

pazhamozhi.literal: water that a tank has held a long time

story.act: no story; a long-filled tank stands for long-gathered wealth that giving will not soon drain

pazhamozhi.applied_to: discerning giving from long-gathered wealth does not soon exhaust it

375.reading: The excellent givers are those who see what a suppliant has in mind, judging from his very manner, and give that; the verse tells the lord of cool hills where the owl hoots in the millet field that no one drops a stone into a begging bowl.
375.nuance: The proverb is read as: what goes into the bowl must be what the bowl is for, so the gift must answer the asker's need, and the best giver reads that need before it is spoken.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who puts a stone into a begging bowl

story.act: no story; the alms bowl takes food, not stones

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a gift should fit what the asker needs, which the best giver reads unasked

376.reading: Even when they have nothing left to call people in and give, those long used to giving freely are the ones who can wipe away the distress of those who depend on them, as a great horse, even wasted, shows its difference once it is in harness.
376.nuance: தூஉய்ப் பயின்றார் is read as those practised in scattering (giving lavishly); it could also mean those practised in purity. வாய்ப்புத்தான் before the quotation is hard to construe.

pazhamozhi.proverb: வாடியக் கண்ணும் பெருங்குதிரை யாப்புள்வே றாகி விடும்
pazhamozhi.literal: even when it has wasted, a great horse becomes distinct in its harness

story.act: no story; the thoroughbred, though thin, shows its breed once harnessed

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the habitual giver keeps relieving his dependents even when his means are gone

377.reading: Let those who came to one who gave a thing to each who asked go off saying they have made him poor; the verse tells a woman with five-plaited hair that, for anyone at all, there is no one who has become poor by giving.
377.nuance: கொண்டார் is read as the takers who leave thinking they have stripped the giver; it could also be his own people who complain that he has ruined them. அடுத்தேறல் in the address is obscure.

pazhamozhi.literal: there are none who became poor by giving

story.act: no story; the proverb denies that giving impoverishes

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving does not impoverish the giver, whatever onlookers say

378.reading: Have those who conceal their wealth, thinking it will dwindle if they give to askers, never seen for themselves, the verse asks the lord of the shore where a boat rides at the landing on the swelling sea, that a well springs fresh each time it is drawn?

pazhamozhi.literal: the well springs up each time it is drawn

story.act: no story; a well refills as water is drawn from it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving does not diminish wealth but renews it

379.reading: Only the foolish say a gift goes by the rank of the suppliants; the deeds of patrons who, concealing nothing, have worn generosity as their ornament are all great in the measure of their own worth, as a water-flower rises to the measure of the water.
379.nuance: The verse moves the measure of a gift from the receiver to the giver: வரிசை (rank, due measure) belongs to the patron's சீர், not to the suppliant's standing.

pazhamozhi.literal: water flowers are bounded by the water

story.act: no story; a water flower's height follows the depth of water

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a gift's greatness follows the patron's worth, not the suppliant's rank

380.reading: When a great poet had composed his song, a patron, to make good the want spoken in his words, said 'give to him as he asks; may you live long'; there is no need to spell out such men by name, for givers themselves know the measure of their own worth.
380.nuance: The first two lines seem to tell a particular episode of a patron answering a poet, but neither is named; அடுத்தர and தொடுத்தின்னார் என்னலோ வேண்டா are hard to construe, so the episode is reported only as far as the words allow.

pazhamozhi.literal: givers themselves know the measure of their own worth

story.act: a patron answers a great poet's composition by bidding that he be given what he lacks and blessing him

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a true giver gives by the measure of his own worth without needing to be told

381.reading: Even in a time of drought without rain, Pari's young daughter gave a bard gold, putting it in the pot of water on the fire to serve as his food; there is no doorstep to which nothing at all comes.
381.nuance: The proverb can be read two ways: every house, even in drought, has something to give, or every house will in time receive something. The episode of gold put in the cooking pot in place of rice is the verse's own; it does not say the daughter was poor, only that the rain had failed.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no front yard where nothing comes

story.act: in a rainless season Pari's young daughter put gold in the pot of water and gave it to a bard as his food

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving goes on in every house, even when the means of giving fail

382.reading: For the strong, whose generosity makes even their foes hand over what they own so that fame stays with all who receive, and who can encircle and take their foes' land, what is hard to give? The man who has a daughter does not fear loss.
382.nuance: The proverb's father has already reckoned with giving his daughter away, so loss holds no fear for him; the verse applies this to the conquering king, for whom wealth given is wealth that can be won again. மண்ணசுற்றிக் looks corrupt, and the first two lines are hard to construe.

pazhamozhi.literal: he who has begotten a girl does not fear loss

story.act: no story; the father of a daughter is resigned to giving her away

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a king strong enough to take what he gives does not fear the cost of giving

383.reading: The giving of those who give lavishly without regard to return and without discernment, looking only to fame, is, the verse tells the lord of the cool shore where the sea leaps roaring like strong horses, the way of working for wages and eating.
383.nuance: பயன்நோக்காது seems to clear these givers of seeking return, but the proverb turns it back: fame is their wage, so giving aimed at fame is still paid work. பாத்தறிவு, the sense that divides the deserving from the rest, is what they lack.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way of working for hire and eating

story.act: no story; the hired labourer eats by his wage

pazhamozhi.applied_to: giving for fame is wages, not giving

384.reading: Even a man who never refuses, when many ask him for the same one thing, thinks of the distress of those who will go without and, unable to bear it, hides even what he has; so for living by begging, numbers are bad.
384.nuance: The giver's concealment here comes from pity, not meanness: he hides the one thing because he cannot bear to disappoint the rest. The proverb's counsel falls on the askers.

pazhamozhi.literal: for eating by begging, many together is bad

story.act: no story; a crowd of askers defeats the one they ask

pazhamozhi.applied_to: suppliants who come in numbers make even a generous giver withhold

385.reading: People of great show and great desire who attach themselves to those who cannot satisfy that desire are, the verse tells a woman with heavy earrings and kohl-lined eyes like the river's kayal, going the way of axle grease that soaks in and is gone.
385.nuance: The image of axle grease that sinks into the wheel and is lost is read as the suppliant's hope and effort spent for nothing; தோற்றம் பெரிய may describe either the seekers' show or the patrons'.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way axle grease sinks in

story.act: no story; grease rubbed on an axle soaks away

pazhamozhi.applied_to: seeking from a patron who cannot give wastes the seeker

386.reading: When vast wealth slips its guard and runs off and a great king seizes it, what can those who never gave it away do? Even for great renouncers, when overwhelming things befall, there is no remedy.
386.nuance: The proverb is read as saying that excess, whether of wealth or of misfortune, admits no cure, so wealth should be given before the king takes it; நீத்தப் பெரியார் widens the point to renouncers, which fits the heading only loosely.

pazhamozhi.literal: when excessive things arrive there is no remedy

story.act: no story; the hoard swept away to a seizing king

pazhamozhi.applied_to: wealth not given in time is lost past remedy

links.note: Naladiyar 98 calls giving to those who will give back a profitable loan; Pazhamozhi 372 shows the same giving as bait cast to land a larger fish.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar names the return-seeking gift a loan between equals; Pazhamozhi adds the disproportion, a small gift aimed at a large catch, so the fault is not only expecting return but calculating a profit on it.
links.list_adds: its angler's image adds the ratio of small outlay to large gain that the quatrain's loan does not state.

links.note: Kural 1009 says others take wealth amassed without love or virtue; Pazhamozhi 373 names the taker, the seizing king, and sets the small gift to the destitute against the hoard.
links.teaches: The Kural leaves the taker as 'others'; Pazhamozhi makes him the king who drives the hoarder out, and pairs the lost hoard with rain in the wilderness, so the choice is between feeding royal power and feeding the destitute.
links.list_adds: it sets two ends of wealth side by side, the hoard going to the king and a single gift going to the starving, which the couplet's one fate does not contrast.

links.note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to water filling the village tank; Pazhamozhi 374 uses the tank to say discerning giving from long-gathered wealth does not quickly drain it.
links.teaches: The Kural's tank is wealth open to all; Pazhamozhi's tank is wealth that lasts though drawn on, so the same image answers the giver's fear of exhaustion, on condition that a capable man gives with discernment.
links.list_adds: it adds to the tank image the time it took to fill and the skill of the one who gives from it, so lasting depends on how the wealth was gathered and how it is given.

links.note: Kural 1052 says asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering; Pazhamozhi 375 calls excellent the giver who reads the asker's mind and gives what he wants.
links.teaches: The Kural conditions the asker's pleasure on getting without pain; Pazhamozhi locates the means in the giver, who spares that pain by reading the need from the asker's manner and giving the fit thing, not stones for the bowl.
links.list_adds: its begging-bowl proverb adds that the gift must match the need, a requirement on what is given that the couplet does not make.

links.note: Kural 218 says those who know what is due do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even without means; Pazhamozhi 376 says those long used to giving still relieve dependents when they have nothing to give.
links.teaches: Read together, the Kural gives the reason, knowledge of what is due, and Pazhamozhi gives the source, long habit of giving, so the giving that survives poverty is both understood and practised into the body like a horse's training.
links.list_adds: its thin-but-harnessed horse adds that the capacity shows only when put to work, a point the couplet's bare statement lacks.

links.note: Naladiyar 141 says the well-born in rags keep their principles, as a starving lion will not eat grass; Pazhamozhi 376 says the habitual giver, wasted, still relieves his dependents, as a thin great horse shows in harness.
links.teaches: Both use a noble animal reduced by want; the Naladiyar's lion shows what the noble will not do, Pazhamozhi's horse what he still does, so poverty is shown to test both refusal and service.
links.list_adds: it turns the quatrain's refusal into a positive act, relieving others' distress, so the proof of nobility in want becomes giving rather than abstaining.

links.note: Kural 220 grants for argument that ruin may come by ஒப்புரவு and calls it worth buying with oneself; Pazhamozhi 377 denies that anyone has ever become poor by giving.
links.teaches: The Kural meets the objection by accepting the cost; Pazhamozhi meets it by denying the cost exists, so the two show two answers to the fear that giving ruins, one heroic and one reassuring.
links.list_adds: its proverb flatly denies the premise the couplet entertains, and places the claim of ruin in the mouths of the takers rather than the giver.

links.note: Kural 228 asks whether the hard-eyed who hoard and lose do not know the joy of giving; Pazhamozhi 378 asks whether those who hide wealth fearing it will dwindle have not seen the well refill.
links.teaches: Both ask the hoarder 'do they not know', but the Kural points to the joy he misses and Pazhamozhi to the fact he misjudges, that drawing renews the source, so the hoarder is wrong about both pleasure and arithmetic.
links.list_adds: its well proverb supplies the hoarder's own reason, fear of dwindling, and answers it with a fact of nature the couplet does not use.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 374's tank does not quickly run dry; 378's well springs fresh each time it is drawn.
links.teaches: The tank says giving does not soon exhaust stored wealth; the well says drawing on it renews it, so within one chapter the claim rises from endurance to replenishment.

links.note: Kural 595 says a water-flower rises to the water's depth and a man's height to his mind; Pazhamozhi 379 uses the same image to say a patron's gifts are great by the measure of his worth.
links.teaches: The Kural measures a man's rise by his inner drive; Pazhamozhi applies the image to giving, so the size of a gift becomes a reading of the giver's worth and not of the suppliant's rank.
links.list_adds: it carries the image from striving to giving and sets it against the foolish view that gifts follow the receiver's rank, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

links.note: 379 says a patron's gifts are great by his own worth; 380 says givers themselves know the measure of their worth and need no prompting.
links.teaches: 379 states that the giver's worth sets the gift; 380 adds that the giver knows that measure himself, so the true patron gives unprompted and the poet need not name or press him.

links.note: Purananuru 116 shows Pari's daughters after his fall, in a thorn-fenced hut counting salt carts; Pazhamozhi 381 shows Pari's daughter giving a bard gold in a drought.
links.teaches: The Purananuru remembers the daughters as the dispossessed; Pazhamozhi keeps one of them as a giver who feeds a bard even when rain fails, so the ethics work turns the elegy of Pari's house into proof that his giving outlived his fortune.

links.note: 376 says habitual givers relieve dependents even with nothing left; 381 names Pari's daughter giving gold in a drought.
links.teaches: 376 states the rule in general with a horse; 381 gives it a named case from the most famous house of givers, so the chapter pairs the principle with its exemplar.

links.note: Kural 221 calls every gift but one to the destitute a measured loan; Pazhamozhi 383 says even lavish giving with no eye to return is wage labour if it looks to fame.
links.teaches: The Kural strips the name of giving from gifts that expect a material return; Pazhamozhi strips it also from gifts that expect only fame, so the wage can be praise as well as goods.
links.list_adds: it adds fame as a hidden return and names lack of discernment as the giver's fault, which the couplet's loan does not cover.

links.note: Kural 1051 says that if the worthy giver withholds, the blame is his and not the asker's; Pazhamozhi 384 shows a never-refusing giver hiding what he has because many ask one thing, and puts the fault on the crowd of askers.
links.teaches: The Kural places the blame for withholding on the giver; Pazhamozhi names a case where withholding comes from pity for those who would be turned away, so the blame moves to the number of askers.
links.list_adds: its proverb adds the askers' number as a cause of withholding, a condition the couplet's single asker and single giver leave out.

links.note: Naladiyar 126 likens attaching to one thought worthy who is not to opening a casket for sandal and finding a snake; Pazhamozhi 385 likens seekers who attach to patrons unable to satisfy them to axle grease that soaks away.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's failed attachment brings danger, Pazhamozhi's brings slow waste, so the pair shows two costs of attaching without examining: harm from the unworthy and loss to the incapable.
links.list_adds: it moves the quatrain's failed choice of a friend into the suppliant's choice of a patron, and names the seeker's own great desire as the cause.

links.note: 373 says the concealed hoard ends as provision for seizing kings; 386 says wealth that escapes its guard and is seized by a great king leaves those who did not give with no remedy.
links.teaches: 373 sets the hoard's end against the gift's use; 386 adds the hoarder's helplessness after the seizure, so the king's taking appears in the chapter twice, as the hoard's fate and as the moment past remedy.

source_issues: 372: the quotation mark opens inside the word வேண்(டு)'அயிரை, so the proverb's first word is split by the mark.
378: துறைக்தோணி is likely a misprint for துறைத்தோணி.
382: மண்ணசுற்றிக் looks corrupt; the sense of encircling or removing the foes' land is guessed.
384: பெறாஅஅன் has a doubled alapedai vowel, likely a misprint for பெறாஅன்.
